item.title: Linear Objective Problems: A Complexity Framework for Bilevel Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.11375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many bilevel and robust optimization problems are complete for the second level of the polynomial hierarchy, but such results are usually proven one problem at a time with problem-specific reductions. A recurring obstacle is that the lower level must select an optimal solution rather than merely a feasible one, whereas standard reductions preserve only whether a solution exists, not which solutions are optimal. We introduce linear objective problems (LOP), a framework for optimization problems whose solutions are explicit subsets of a ground set and whose objective is linear in these elements. We define tight solution-embedding reductions, which map the optimal solutions of one problem element by element onto the optimal solutions of another, without having to recognize optimal solutions, which is coNP-hard in general. This gives a notion of LOP-completeness, with Satisfiability as the canonical complete problem, even with unit weights. We show that many classical problems are LOP-complete, including Vertex Cover, Dominating Set, TSP, Knapsack, and Steiner Tree, and we introduce a duality that transfers LOP-completeness between minimization and maximization problems. As our main application, we prove a meta-theorem for min-max regret optimization under interval uncertainty: for every LOP-complete problem, the min-max regret version is $\Sigma_2^p$-complete. Instead of a separate proof for each nominal problem, it suffices to show that the nominal problem is LOP-complete. This recovers known results for the interval min-max regret versions of Knapsack and Maximum Benefit Set Cover and yields completeness for over 50 further problems.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Gr\"une, James B. Orlin, Lasse Wulf

item.title: On the Complexity of Extending Prescribed Linear Forests to Hamiltonian Cycles in Hypercubes
item.description: arXiv:2611.11476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let $Q_n$ be the $n$-dimensional hypercube, and let $P\subseteq E(Q_n)$ be a set of prescribed edges. It is known that, for $n\ge 2$, every such set $P$ with $|P|\leq 2n-3$ whose edges form a linear forest is contained in a Hamiltonian cycle of $Q_n$. This bound is sharp for general linear forests. The computational complexity of deciding whether a prescribed edge set of a hypercube can be extended to a Hamiltonian cycle was posed as an open question by Dvo\v{r}\'ak [SIAM J. Discrete Math. 19 (2005) 135--144]. We prove that the problem is NP-complete even when the prescribed edges form a spanning linear forest with no isolated vertices. We give a polynomial-time reduction from a restricted 3-SAT problem, using local spanning path-forest gadgets for variables and clauses that are uniformly embedded in the hypercube. The same reduction therefore establishes NP-hardness of two versions of Hamiltonian-cycle extension problems for general prescribed edge sets.
item.dc:creator: Huazhong L\"{u}, Tingzeng Wu

item.title: A note on exact external information complexity
item.description: arXiv:2611.11488v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the prior-free zero-error private-coin external information complexity $B(f)$ of finite two-party functions, with correctness on every input. An elementary rectangle/entropy argument gives $B(\mathsf{AND})=\log_2 3$. A complete classification of Boolean $3\times3$ matrices leaves, up to input permutations and output complementation, only the two-overlapping-rectangles function $F$ without an exact value. An entropy potential and a finite rational protocol give $2.1212661667060486842\ldots\le B(F)<2.130998318$. We also determine its deterministic external information and zero-error communication costs. A separate product-prior certificate and internal-information additivity yield $R_0^{\mathrm{pub}}(F^{\times t})\ge2.021991187178562\ldots\,t$, strictly exceeding the fractional-cover rate $2t$.
item.dc:creator: Henning Wunderlich

item.title: Closing the Complexity Gap for Wheeler Graph Recognition on $d$-NFAs
item.description: arXiv:2611.11572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wheeler graph recognition asks whether a directed graph whose arcs are labeled by symbols from a totally ordered alphabet admits a Wheeler order, a total order on its vertices compatible with the labels of arcs and the order of their tails. A $d$-NFA is a nondeterministic finite automaton in which at most $d$ transitions with any given label leave each state. For Wheeler graph recognition on $d$-NFAs, Alanko et al. gave a polynomial-time algorithm for $d \leq 2$, whereas Gibney and Thankachan proved NP-completeness for every fixed $d \geq 5$. The computational complexity for $d = 3$ and $d = 4$ remained open. We resolve both open cases by extending the reduction of Gibney and Thankachan with a new encoding of clauses of Not-All-Equal 3-SAT. Specifically, we prove that recognition is NP-complete even for directed acyclic graphs over an ordered binary alphabet with a unique source reaching every vertex and total out-degree at most three at every vertex. Consequently, Wheeler graph recognition on $d$-NFAs is NP-complete for every fixed $d \geq 3$.
item.dc:creator: Kengo Hashimoto

item.title: Simulating Nondeterministic Turing Machines in Subexponential Deterministic Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.11832v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that every multitape nondeterministic Turing machine can be simulated deterministically in subexponential time. Specifically, we show that the recent algorithms for $3$-$\mathsf{SAT}$ presented by OpenAI and Anthropic imply $\mathsf{NTIME}[t]\subseteq\mathsf{DTIME}[2^{O(t \log \log t/\sqrt{\log t})}]$, and that a stronger consequence of their proof yields \[\mathsf{NTIME}[t] \subseteq\mathsf{DTIME}[2^{O(t /\sqrt{\log t})}]. \] More generally, we show that any subexponential time algorithm for solving circuit-CSPs transfers to a deterministic simulation of $\mathsf{NTIME}$ with the same savings. Our results follow from new generalizations of Cook--Levin, which may be of independent interest.
item.dc:creator: Carmen Strassle, Bernardo Subercaseaux

item.title: On Non-Deterministic Representation of Boolean Functions
item.description: arXiv:2611.11966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study non-deterministic representation of Boolean functions by polynomials, introduced by (de Wolf, 2000). A polynomial $p(x)$ is said to be a non-deterministic polynomial for a Boolean function $f$ if for all $a\in\{0,1\}^n$, $p(a)\neq 0$ iff $f(a)=1$. The non-deterministic degree of $f$, denoted $\mathsf{ndeg}(f)$, is the minimal degree of a non-deterministic polynomial for $f$. In this work, we show the following main results: - Almost all Boolean functions on $n$ variables have non-deterministic degree at most $n/2 + O(\sqrt{n\log n})$. This confirms a conjecture of (Iyer et al., 2023). Together with the lower bound of (Iyer et al., 2023) it establishes a tight bound on the rational degree of a random Boolean function up to lower order terms. - We disprove a conjecture of (Kothari et al., 2026) about effective hypercube nullstellensatz for more than two polynomials. On the positive side, we also identify a constraint under which an effective hypercube nullstellensatz holds for many polynomials.
item.dc:creator: Sudharshan Rajagopalan, Nitin Saurabh

item.title: Polynomial Sample Complexity of Noninteractive Simulation over Finite Alphabets
item.description: arXiv:2611.11974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study noninteractive simulation from a finite correlated source. Alice and Bob observe independent copies of the source and generate outputs without communication. We give a quantitative construction for arbitrary finite output alphabets: for every fixed source, a joint law that is simulable with arbitrarily many samples can be approximated using a number of samples polynomial jointly in the output alphabet sizes and the inverse accuracy. We first study binary outputs. A one-sided Wright--Fisher comparison gives a source-dependent explicit exponent and a finite-head Gaussian-threshold representation. We then handle arbitrary finite output alphabets through averaged influence regularity, simplex-preserving Gaussian moment lifting, and a common Gaussian projection for all correlated-prefix states. The sample exponent is independent of the output alphabet sizes. For a concrete biased binary source we certify an explicit exponent below $19$.
item.dc:creator: Haoran Wang

item.title: Type-logical grammars and formal languages
item.description: arXiv:2611.12618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that type-logical grammars with the standard rules for product, associativity, extraction and infixation have an NP-complete fixed recognition problem, adapting a construction for first-order linear logic from Pshenitsyn (2025), who already showed that grammars in first-order linear logic are closed under intersection and therefore not semilinear and not mildly context-sensitive. We strengthen these results and shown that grammars in first-order linear logic can simulate the quasi-linear grammars of Book \& Greibach (1970), the grammars recognised in non-deterministic linear time (NSPACE(n) or. NLIN). I argue that NLIN is an interesting class of formal languages as well, and a useful upper bound on the time complexity of formalisms used for natural language, just like LOGCFL is a useful upper bound on the space complexity. Taken together this means that first-order linear logic can be seen as the logic of non-deterministic linear-time string languages, graph languages and automata.
item.dc:creator: Richard Moot (LIRMM,CNRS,LIRMM | PIPL,UM)

item.title: The Complexity of Computing Coarse Correlated Equilibria in Markov Games with a Single Controller
item.description: arXiv:2607.10897v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the complexity of computing stationary Markov coarse correlated equilibria (CCE) in discounted single-controller stochastic (Markov) games [PR81, FV97], a fundamental subclass of stochastic games in which all players may affect rewards, but only one player controls the state transitions. Prior work [DGZ23, JMS23, HN25] established PPAD-hardness for computing stationary Markov CCE in two-player general-sum stochastic games via turn-based constructions in which each state is controlled by a single player, with control alternating across states. This structure forces every Markov CCE to collapse to a Nash equilibrium (NE), so hardness for NE transfers immediately to CCE. It remained open whether hardness persists when a single player controls all transitions--a setting where no such collapse occurs. We resolve this question: computing an approximate stationary Markov CCE in two-player single-controller stochastic games is PPAD-complete, even with a fixed discount factor and binary actions. For the perfect notion (equilibrium constraints at every state) this holds unconditionally at constant accuracy; for the non-perfect notion, we prove constant-accuracy hardness under the PCP-for-PPAD hypothesis [BPR16, DFHM26] and inverse-polynomial-accuracy hardness unconditionally. To the best of our knowledge, our result is the first to show hardness for computing CCE without relying on equilibrium collapse phenomena or other routes through Nash-like structure [FGK23, AKSZ24, PR24]. Instead, we construct single-controller gadgets whose local incentive constraints force a solution of a Pure-Circuit instance even under strongly correlated stationary policies.
item.dc:creator: Gabriele Farina, Andreas Kontogiannis, Ioannis Panageas, Vasilis Pollatos

item.title: Initialization masks overcome decoding obstructions in compressed QAOA
item.description: arXiv:2611.10588v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In compressed quantum optimization, a variational state is converted into a classical assignment by decoding noncommuting observables. We show that this step creates structural restrictions that changing the initialization can remove, even when increasing circuit depth cannot. For an explicit infinite family of connected cubic graphs on $n=3r$ vertices, with a fixed Pauli encoding and deterministic sign decoder, every all-plus QAOA circuit has cut at most $2r$, at every finite depth and every real angle sequence. A uniform signed product-state mask at fixed depth-one angles has expected cut $13r/4$, an additive advantage $5n/12$; an infinite subfamily admits an optimal mask. A second construction retains a linear depth-one separation under weak weighted couplings, a bounded cost-angle domain and a specified production-encoder ordering. Noiseless simulations then test classical mask selection before energy optimization. On 1,699 random cubic MaxCut instances, one selected mask achieves mean ratio $0.9100$, versus $0.7067$ for the all-plus $X$ baseline and $0.9125$ for the best of $r^2$ separately optimized random masks. On complete cohorts of weighted MaxCut, sparse Ising, Max-2-XOR and Max-2-SAT, the selected mask also improves on the baseline at every size, but it trails the pool at small sizes and leads it significantly only at the larger MaxCut and Ising sizes. Finite-pool order statistics separate the effect of selection from that of drawing a random mask. The results distinguish decoded expressivity from optimized energy and empirical performance; they do not establish a quantum computational advantage.
item.dc:creator: Emilio Semre, Steven Frankel

item.title: A Grover-Amplified Oracle for Maximum Clique on Graph, Minimum Hitting set and Dualizations on Hypergraphs Built on Quantum Phase Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.10640v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we use a quantum circuit called the Graph Encoding Operator which, applied to the complement $\bar G$ of any graph $G$, yields an oracle for the maximum clique problem suitable for amplification via Grover's algorithm. Analogously, we devise a Hypergraph Encoding Operator which, when applied to a hypergraph $\mathcal H$, yields an oracle for the minimum hitting set suitable for amplification via Grover's algorithm. Interestingly, the latter oracle provides, when measured, an approximation of the number of hitting sets of the hypergraph, thus solving the dualization problem for positive Boolean functions represented in a positive irredundant disjunctive normal form. We give the full construction of both operators, prove their correctness, analyze their complexity, and provide an implementation on a quantum simulator. We discuss the resulting complexity, contrast them with existing quantum computer algorithms based on Grover search and we will show that our algorithms outperform, to the best of our knowledge, all of the previous algorithms on space computational complexity by requiring only $O(N)$ number of qubits with respect to the number of vertices $N$, for representing both graphs and hypergraphs in the encoding operator and, consequently, results in an oracle for both graphs and hypergraphs that uses only $O(N)$ qubits even when the hypergraph contains an exponential (on the number of vertices) number of hyperedges.
item.dc:creator: Francisco Pi\~nero, Fernando L. \Pelayo, Hernan I. de la Cruz, Jose J. Paulet, Mauro Mezzini, Fernando Cuartero

item.title: Solving Large Rubik's Cubes within a Factor of $2.37+o(1)$ of Optimal
item.description: arXiv:2611.11018v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We design optimized algorithms to solve the $n \times n \times n$ Rubik's Cube within $30.5 n^2 / \lg n + o(n^2 / \lg n)$ moves. This upper bound is asymptotically within a factor of $2.37$ of the known lower bound, which applies to almost all instances. The constant $30.5$ is also the first explicit constant factor for the known upper bound of $O(n^2 / \lg n)$, where the implicit constant of the previous algorithm was $1.01 \cdot 10^{40}$ (ten duodecillion). Thus we improve the upper-bound constant by a factor of more than $3.30 \cdot 10^{38}$ (330 undecillion). Our algorithm runs in time linear in the input size $N = \Theta(n^2)$, and uses $O(\sqrt{N} \lg N)$ extra space (beyond the state of the cube). Our implementation is the first practical cube solver to generate solutions of length $O(n^2/\lg n)$. Our latest solver outperforms existing solvers for $n$ as small as $840$.
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Mrzyglocki, Tomas Rokicki, Maxine Perroni-Scharf, Erik D. Demaine

item.title: Do Feature Interactions Break Explainability? Provable Explanations for Any-Order Neural Additive Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.11224v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for neural networks are often heuristic and lack provable guarantees. A common alternative to such methods that was studied in recent years is to compute a cardinally-minimal subset of input features that is provably sufficient to determine the model's prediction. For general neural networks, however, finding such explanations is computationally intractable. In contrast, recent work showed that this problem becomes more tractable for a particular family of neural networks, namely neural additive models (NAMs), though standard NAMs are highly restrictive because they exclude feature interactions altogether. In this work, we study the computation of provably minimal and sufficient explanations for neural networks with restricted feature interactions, bridging the gap between fully general neural networks and purely additive models. We first prove that even with constant-order interactions, the problem is $\Sigma_2^P$-hard, implying that worst-case exponential complexity is unavoidable. We then identify two provably tractable settings: one based on sparsity in the interaction structure and another based on a stronger interaction-aware notion of sufficiency. Under either of these settings, we develop algorithms that compute provable explanations for neural networks with any-order interactions while retaining much of the computational efficiency of additive models. Empirically, we show that these explanations are significantly smaller and faster to obtain than those produced by standard algorithms, while being derived from models that achieve much higher accuracy than standard NAMs. Overall, our results help expand the class of neural networks that admit efficient provable explanations, while clarifying the fundamental role of feature interactions in shaping their complexity.
item.dc:creator: Idan Refaeli, Yizhak Yisrael Elboher, Guy Katz, Shahaf Bassan

item.title: Amortized Cell-Probe Lower Bounds for Dynamic Boolean Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.11508v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove the first unconditional amortized $\Omega\big((\log N/\log\log N)^2\big)$ cell-probe lower bound for a Boolean dynamic problem. For insert-only multiphase Disjointness with $N$ query sets over $[N]$ and word size $w=\Theta(\log N)$, a fixed distribution of interleaved insertions and queries forces this expected average cost per operation, excluding preprocessing. The bound allows sufficiently small constant error for each query of every fixed legal sequence and imposes no restriction on individual operation costs. It transfers to incremental directed reachability, incremental subgraph connectivity, and fully dynamic triangle detection. We also prove $t_q=\Omega\big((\log N/\log(t_uw))^2\big)$ for amortized insertion time $1\le t_u=N^{o(1)}$ and expected query time $t_q$, when the number of insertions before the final query is not announced in advance. We reach the quadratic-logarithmic scale with bounded error by combining interleaving with the 2.5-round communication framework [Ko26a, Ko26b] and controlling errors among accepted simulations.
item.dc:creator: Young Kun Ko

item.title: Proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture: An Exposition
item.description: arXiv:2611.11626v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give an exposition of a recent proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which states that every degree-$d$ polynomial $p : \{0,1\}^n \to [0,1]$ has a variable of influence at least $\mathrm{poly}(\mathrm{Var}(p)/d)$. This implies that quantum query algorithms for decision problems can be efficiently simulated classically on most inputs. It also yields a near-equivalence between the status of the $\mathsf{BPP}$ vs. $\mathsf{BQP}$ problem in the random oracle and unrelativized worlds. We organize the proof around four main steps and discuss how each connects to the literature on the analysis of boolean functions and probabilistic combinatorics. To bring out the key ideas, we do not optimize parameters, and our presentation yields weaker exponents than the original. $\textbf{Authors' note.}$ The proof was discovered by David Turturean using a research system developed at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), in combination with a non-public Anthropic model. The proof was then shared with the authors, who worked to understand it and prepare this exposition. Anthropic's public models were used in this process. The authors did not receive financial compensation from Anthropic or PSI. This article is not intended for publication at a conference or in a journal.
item.dc:creator: Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle, Li-Yang Tan

item.title: Strong Backdoor to Forests is FPT: Tight Linear-Time FPT for Essentially General SAT
item.description: arXiv:2611.12321v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In a seminal work, Gaspers and Szeider [FOCS 2013] gave a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) approximate algorithm for finding a strong backdoor of size at most $k$ to incidence treewidth at most $t$, for a given CNF-formula $\phi$. In particular, their algorithm runs in $f(k,t) |\phi|^3$ time, and finds a strong backdoor to treewidth at most $t$, of $\phi$, of size at most $2^k$ whenever there exists one of size at most $k$. Determining whether the detection of strong backdoors to bounded incidence treewidth is FPT parameterized by $k+t$ was left open in their work and this has been repeatedly posed as an open question by Gaspers and Szeider, for example in [The Multivariate Algorithmic Revolution and Beyond 2012] and more recently in [Computer Science Reviews 2025], even for incidence forests and when the input is a $3$-CNF formula. We answer this question affirmatively. We show that strong backdoors to forests can be found in linear-FPT time on arbitrary non-tautological CNF formulas (not just on 3-CNF formulas). Given such a formula $\phi$ and a budget $k$, our algorithm finds a strong backdoor to the class of forests, of size at most $k$, or correctly reports that none exists, in $2^{2^{O(k)}} |\phi|$ time. Moreover, we show that our result is as tight as it can get. First, we show that finding strong backdoors to treewidth $t$ for any $t \geq 2$ is W[1]-hard, even on non-tautological 3-CNF formulas. Second, the running time of our algorithm is tight: it is linear in the input size and a better than double-exponential dependence on $k$ in the running time would imply a $2^{o(N/\log N)}$-time algorithm for solving 3-SAT on $N$ variables, which would beat even the very recently claimed sub-exponential algorithm for solving 3-SAT by OpenAI and Anthropic.
item.dc:creator: Olesia Bilyk, Aidar Munduzbaev, Roohani Sharma, Mamnoon Siam

item.title: Polynomial-Space Quantum Algorithms from Classical Branching: Colouring, Domination and Monotone Local Search
item.description: arXiv:2611.12714v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give quantum algorithms for exponential-time problems on $n$ vertices or elements, with bounded error, polynomial space and no quantum random access memory. Our results are these. (1) 4-Colouring in quantum time $O(1.3032^n)$, from a polynomial-space branching algorithm with polynomial-space terminal algorithms; with the branching algorithm alone, $O(1.3100^n)$. The previous best bound in this model, to our knowledge, is $O(1.3231^n)$. (2) $k$-Colouring below the previous best bound for $k \in \{5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11\}$ and $13 \le k \le 18$, from $O(1.4518^n)$ for $k = 5$ to $O(1.9233^n)$ for $k = 18$. (3) Dominating Set in $O(1.2235^n)$, against the previous $O(2^{n/2})$, Independent Dominating Set in $O(1.1583^n)$, and Edge Dominating Set and Minimum Maximal Matching in $O(1.1501^n)$. (4) A quantum form of monotone local search: if the extension problem has a backtracking tree with $c^k$ nodes up to polynomial factors, the problem is solved in quantum time $(2 - 1/c)^{n/2}$ up to polynomial factors. This gives Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3081^n)$, Subset and Group Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.3229^n)$, Cluster Vertex Deletion in $O(1.2033^n)$, 3-Hitting Set in $O(1.2405^n)$, Proper Interval Vertex Deletion in $O(1.3541^n)$, Multicut on Trees in $O(1.1647^n)$ and Min-Ones $d$-SAT in $O^*((2-1/d)^{n/2})$. (5) Quantum exponential-time approximations below the quantum exact bounds, such as a 1.1-approximation for Vertex Cover in $O(1.0555^n)$ and for Feedback Vertex Set in $O(1.2161^n)$. The colouring exponents for $k \ge 6$ come from an evaluation of a known reduction recursion, computed in floating point with a margin.
item.dc:creator: Sebastian Senge

item.title: $\mathsf{EQP}\subseteq\mathsf{IP}$ Does Not Relativize
item.description: arXiv:2611.12746v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We construct a recursive oracle $O$ and a unary language $L\in\mathsf{EQP}^O\setminus(\mathsf{IP}^O\cup\mathsf{PH}^O)$, strengthening the $\mathsf{BQP}$ versus $\mathsf{IP}$ oracle separation of Bouland et al. to exact quantum computation. The separation is based on a variant of the Forrelation problem in which the normalized correlation of one Boolean function with the Fourier transform of another is promised to be exactly $+1/2$ or $-1/2$. The main technical contribution is a repair method that constructs distributions supported on these exact levels while preserving the indistinguishability needed for the $\mathsf{IP}$ and $\mathsf{PH}$ lower bounds. A uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm distinguishes the two cases with certainty using only three oracle queries.
item.dc:creator: Sinan Oral, Supartha Podder

item.title: Succinct Infinite-Horizon Lyapunov and LQR Value Problems Are BQP-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2611.12757v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fundamental tasks in linear systems analysis and control require evaluating infinite-horizon output energies for autonomous systems and optimal value functions for controlled systems. These quantities are characterized by Lyapunov and algebraic Riccati equations, respectively. In this work, we study promise problems for their evaluation when the system matrices are sparse and represented succinctly by Boolean circuits specifying their nonzero entries, with input length polynomial in the logarithm of the system dimension. For dissipative autonomous systems with coordinate-vector initial states, we define the succinct Lyapunov value problem (SLV). Its extension to linear-quadratic optimal control is the succinct LQR value problem (SLQRV). We prove that SLV is $\BQP$-hard: every problem in bounded-error quantum polynomial time ($\BQP$) reduces to it in polynomial time. We then establish that the more general SLQRV problem admits a quantum algorithm running in time polynomial in the succinct input length. Since SLV is a special case of SLQRV, both problems are $\BQP$-complete. Consequently, unless bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time coincides with $\BQP$, no classical randomized algorithm can solve either problem on all promised instances in time polynomial in the succinct input length.
item.dc:creator: Mohamed Serry, Jun Liu

item.title: A short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture via the completion framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.12795v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give a short proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture. If a partial Boolean function $f$ is defined on a $\delta$-fraction of all $n$-bit strings and have quantum query complexity $Q(f)$, then, for every $0<\epsilon<1$, a deterministic algorithm computes $f$ correctly on at least a $1-\epsilon$ fraction of its domain using $O( Q(f)^6 / (\epsilon \delta)^2)$ queries. Our proof uses the completion framework and establishes a more general bound in terms of the classical adversary measure. The only result we use from Turturean's recent proof is a special case of his certificate inequality, for which we provide a self-contained proof. We also derive the stronger variant of the Aaronson-Ambainis Conjecture, the bounded-polynomial influence conjecture, from our main result in the appendix.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Huffstutler, David Miloschewsky, Supartha Podder

item.title: Computing the Elementary Symmetric Polynomials in Positive Characteristics
item.description: arXiv:2509.05009v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We first extend the results of Chatterjee, Kumar, Shi, Volk (Computational Complexity 2022) by showing that the degree-$d$ elementary symmetric polynomials in $n$ variables have arithmetic formula lower bounds of $\Omega(d(n-d))$ over fields of positive characteristic. This is done by characterizing the dimension of the singular locus of the elementary symmetric polynomials in positive characteristic fields (parts of the characterization only hold over infinite fields). Then, we show that the results of the universality of border fan-in-two $\Sigma\Pi\Sigma$-circuits from Kumar (ACM Trans. Comput. Theory 2020) over zero-characteristic fields do not extend to fields of positive characteristic. This is done through studying linear projections of the elementary symmetric polynomial as studied by Shpilka (Journal of Computer and System Sciences 2002).
item.dc:creator: Ian Orzel

item.title: Local Search with Correlated Randomness
item.description: arXiv:2607.17469v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The running-time distribution of a randomized algorithm is computed under independent randomness, but independence is rarely what a source guarantees. We study sources $\nu$ with $\nu[w]\le DP[w]^s$ for every finite prefix $w$ of the tape, where $P$ is an independent reference law, $0<s\le1$, and $D\ge1$; individual choices may be predictable, even determined by the past. The worst-case probability of any closed tape event $E$ is exactly $\min\{1,DC_s(E)\}$, where $C_s(E)$ is the infimum cost of covering $E$ by prefixes of varying depth. This tree max-flow/min-cut identity makes worst-case probabilities exact and optimizable. Three applications follow. In scheduling, $n$ tasks on one machine are each retried until the next random symbol lies in its success set; every schedule has the same makespan distribution under independent randomness, yet under our constraint two fixed orders miss a linear deadline with worst-case probabilities $1$ and $\exp[-\Theta(n)]$, and a static priority rule is optimal at every deadline. For the standard local walk on a $k$-CNF with an assignment satisfying a majority of each clause, we find the sharp source threshold $s_*$: below it, on some instances one admissible source forces nontermination for every clause selection; at it, with fixed $D$, the expected number of flips is at most cubic in the initial distance, against linear under independence, with matching instances at distances up to a constant fraction of the number of variables; a fixed margin above it restores linear dependence. For noisy predecessor search with prefix-bounded comparison errors, verified backtracking attains any prescribed error probability at or above a source threshold whose sharpness we leave open, with the same cubic-to-linear query bounds. Restarting on the shared tape restores exponential tails exactly when the nontermination event has a prefix cover of cost below one.
item.dc:creator: Yunbei Xu

item.title: Polynomial-Factor Deterministic NP-Hardness for SVP in Every $\ell_p$ Norm with $p>2$
item.description: arXiv:2608.14529v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove that for every constant $2<p<\infty$, the shortest vector problem in the $\ell_p$ norm is NP-hard to approximate within a polynomial factor under a deterministic reduction. More precisely, for lattices of rank $M$, we obtain a factor of $M^\varepsilon$ for every constant $0<\varepsilon<\min\{(p-2)/(4p),1/8\}$. For $p=\infty$, the same holds for every constant $0<\varepsilon<1/8$. Our reduction adapts OpenAI's encoding of a satisfying assignment for the closest vector problem ("Ten Advances in Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science"). The encoding has one block of coordinates for each evaluation of a polynomial, with one position for each possible value. We allow the entries in a block to be arbitrary field elements, which can cancel when we take weighted sums of powers of these values. We show that on an unsatisfiable formula, a nonzero codeword with small support must have many nonzero entries in each block it uses. Applying a Hadamard matrix to each block, as in a work by Hair and Sahai (STOC 2026), gives the gap in vector length. The main results of this paper were discovered by Codex / ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Ultra using harness components from the UCLA Moonshot Harness Project, in response to a general strategy suggested by the authors. See the end of the introduction for a discussion.
item.dc:creator: Isaac M Hair, Amit Sahai

item.title: Hitting sets From Derivations: Waring Rank and Noncommutative ABPs
item.description: arXiv:2609.34436v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give an explicit hitting set of size $\operatorname{poly}(n,d,r)$ for the class of $n$-variate degree-$d$ polynomials whose partial derivative space is bounded by $r$, over any field $\mathbb{F}$ of characteristic zero (or large enough). In particular, this yields a polynomial sized hitting set for the class of depth-$3$ powering circuits. The proof extends to the setting of noncommutative ABPs and provides a polynomial sized hitting set (of matrices) for the class of noncommututive polynomials that can be computed by polynomial sized noncommutative ABPs (this was also one of the results reported by Open AI~\cite{OpenAI26} in their release on 6 Oct 2026). The main technical insight is the construction of a ``formal derivation'' and properties of the associated Wronskian with respect to this derivation, which was previously studied by Moura \cite{Moura_2004} in a very different context. The proofs in this paper are elementary and completely self-contained. AI disclosure: A subset of the stewards obtained a weaker statement (hitting sets for polynomials with bounded partial derivative space) during conversations \cite{astra_proof} with OpenAI GPT-6 Astra. Extensions of this idea to the broader class of noncommutative ABPs were obtained by the other stewards (via further conversations with Astra), prior to OpenAI's dump on 6 Oct 2026. The proofs presented in this writeup is a rewriting (in the authors' words) of the proofs for both settings obtained by the models in a form that we believe is understandable to researchers. Although the proof is technically identical to OpenAI's release, we believe this exposition is self-contained, simpler, and more valuable to the community. The absurdity of the situation is not lost on us.
item.dc:creator: Shubham Bhardwaj, Foram Lakhani, Partha Mukhopadhyay, Ramprasad Saptharishi, Pratik Shastri, Amit Kumar Sinhababu

item.title: Hardness of Unique Shortest Vectors and Bounded Distance Decoding
item.description: arXiv:2611.09497v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove randomized NP-hardness of the unique shortest vector problem (uSVP) at every constant uniqueness factor greater than one, and of bounded distance decoding (BDD) at every fixed positive fraction less than one half of the minimum distance, in both their threshold decision and search versions. Both results hold in every fixed $\ell_p$ norm with $1\le p<\infty$. Previous Euclidean NP-hardness results for the search versions reached uniqueness factors tending to one and decoding radii greater than the minimum distance divided by $\sqrt2$. For linear codes over every fixed finite field and each fixed ${0<\rho\le1/2}$, the decision version of BDD with radius strictly less than $\rho$ times the minimum distance is equivalent under deterministic polynomial-time reductions to satisfiability for circuits promised to have at most one satisfying input. It is therefore NP-hard under randomized polynomial-time reductions. Earlier hardness for decoding general codes applied beyond half the minimum distance. For every fixed $p>2$ and for $p=\infty$, there is a constant $\epsilon>0$ such that, under randomized polynomial-time reductions, uSVP in the $\ell_p$ norm is NP-hard at uniqueness factor $n^\epsilon$, and BDD in the $\ell_p$ norm is NP-hard at radius $\lambda_1/n^\epsilon$, where $n$ is the lattice rank and $\lambda_1$ is its minimum distance.
item.dc:creator: Sergei Kudria, Jason Luo

item.title: The Trichotomy of Regular Property Testing
item.description: arXiv:2504.19152v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Property testing is concerned with the design of algorithms making a sublinear number of queries to distinguish whether the input satisfies a given property or is far from having this property. A seminal paper of Alon, Krivelevich, Newman, and Szegedy in 2001 introduced property testing of formal languages: the goal is to determine whether an input word belongs to a given language, or is far from any word in that language. They constructed the first property testing algorithm for the class of all regular languages. This opened a line of work with improved complexity results and applications to streaming algorithms. In this work, we show a trichotomy result: the class of regular languages can be divided into three classes, each associated with an optimal query complexity. Our analysis, which reasons directly and combinatorially on automata, yields effective characterizations of all three classes using so-called minimal blocking sequences.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Bathie, Nathana\"el Fijalkow, Corto Mascle

item.title: Exact Quantum Circuit Optimization is co-NQP-hard
item.description: arXiv:2510.16420v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As quantum computing resources remain scarce and error rates high, minimizing the resource consumption of quantum circuits is essential for achieving practical quantum advantage. Here we consider the natural problem of, given a circuit $C$, computing a circuit $C'$ that behaves equivalently on a desired subspace, and that minimizes a quantum resource type, expressed as the count or depth of (i) all gates, or (ii) non-Clifford gates, or (iii) superposition gates, or (iv) entanglement gates. We show that, when $C$ is expressed over any gate-set that can implement the H and TOF gates exactly, a standard property of approximately universal gate-sets, each of the above optimization problems is hard for co-NQP, and hence outside the Polynomial Hierarchy, unless the Polynomial Hierarchy collapses. This complements a recent result of Van de Wetering and Amy (arXiv, 2023) which establishes an NP-hardness lower bound when equivalence is over the full state space, and tightens the gap to the corresponding $\text{NP}^\text{NQP}$ upper bound known for cases (i)-(iii) over Clifford+T and (i)-(iv) over H+TOF circuits. Our result also generalizes a result by Tanaka (Int. J. Quantum Inf., 2010) to other gate-sets and quantum resources.
item.dc:creator: Adam Husted Kjelstr{\o}m, Andreas Pavlogiannis, Jaco van de Pol

item.title: Parameterized Complexity of Stationarity Testing for Piecewise-Affine Functions and Shallow CNN Losses
item.description: arXiv:2605.10219v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the parameterized complexity of testing approximate first-order stationarity at a prescribed point for continuous piecewise-affine (PA) functions, a basic task in nonsmooth optimization. PA functions form a canonical model for nonsmooth stationarity testing and capture the local polyhedral geometry that appears in ReLU-type training losses. Recent work of Tian and So (2025) shows that testing approximate stationarity notions for PA functions is computationally intractable in the worst case, and identifies fixed-dimensional tractability as an open direction. We address this direction from the viewpoint of parameterized complexity, with the ambient dimension $d$ as the parameter. In this paper, we give XP algorithms in fixed dimension for the tractable sides, and prove W[1]-hardness for the complementary sides. Moreover, lower bounds under the parameterized $k$-Clique hypothesis rule out deterministic algorithms running in time $\rho(d)s^{o(d)}$ for any computable function $\rho$, where $s$ denotes the total binary encoding length of the instance. As a further consequence, our results yield the corresponding parameterized complexity picture for testing local minimality of continuous PA functions. We also extend our hardness results to a family of shallow ReLU CNN training losses, tested in the trainable weight space. Thus, the same parameterized-complexity picture also appears for simple CNN training losses. Notably, our lower bounds assume that $k$-Clique on $N$-vertex graphs admits no deterministic $\rho(k)N^{o(k)}$-time algorithm for any computable function $\rho$. The recent refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) (OpenAI, 2026) and the stronger fine-grained $k$-Clique hypothesis (Vassilevska Williams and Zamir, 2026) do not contradict this assumption.
item.dc:creator: Yuhan Ye

item.title: Complexity of Strong Popularity in Hedonic Games
item.description: arXiv:2607.27277v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In a hedonic game, agents are partitioned into coalitions and have preferences over the coalitions they may join. A partition is called strongly popular if it strictly beats every other partition in a majority vote among the agents. We study the complexity of determining the existence of strongly popular partitions in two fundamental classes of hedonic games: additively separable and fractional hedonic games (ASHGs and FHGs), where agents' utilities are determined, respectively, by the sum and average of their valuations for the members of their coalitions. We prove that this problem is PCW-complete for ASHGs and for FHGs even with non-negative valuations, where PCW is a subclass of $\Sigma^P_2$ associated with unambiguous problems (which have at most one witness), recently introduced by Gilboa et al. (2025). These are the first natural complete problems for PCW, in the sense that their formulations do not involve arbitrary Boolean circuits. Our results resolve open problems posed by Brandt and Bullinger (JAIR 2022) and Bullinger and Gilboa (IJCAI 2025). The two reductions employ substantially different techniques, reflecting both the distinct utility models and the stringent non-negativity constraint in FHGs. Furthermore, in contrast with FHGs, we show that in ASHGs restricting valuations to be non-negative makes the problem polynomial-time solvable.
item.dc:creator: Matan Gilboa

item.title: Polyhedral Methods for Cooperative Games: Small Lifts and Hard Faces
item.description: arXiv:2609.24593v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the computational complexity of fundamental algorithmic problems -- membership testing, separation, valid-inequality testing, and linear optimization -- over polytopes and cones arising from cooperative games (also known as pseudo-Boolean functions). A central obstacle in the study of such problems is that a general cooperative game on $n$ players requires $2^n$ values, so the input size is $2^n$ for a game with $n$ players, making these computational tasks theoretically trivial. Restricting to $k$-additive games reduces the input size to $O(n^k)$, making such games a natural target for meaningful questions about the existence of efficient algorithms. On the positive side, we give an explicit extended formulation of size $O(n^k)$ for the core of $k$-additive $k$-monotone games, allowing all four problems to be solved by a single polynomial-size linear program -- in particular, circumventing the ellipsoid method that is needed when building from earlier tractability results of Deng and Papadimitriou, or of Edmonds. For the cone of $k$-additive $(k{-}1)$-monotone games, we give a complete characterization of its extreme rays and derive the same $O(n^k)$ bound on extension complexity, yielding a geometry-based proof and generalization of a result of Billionnet and Minoux. On the negative side, we show that for $l \leq k-2$ the cone of $k$-additive $l$-monotone games is computationally intractable: membership testing is not in NP (unless NP\,=\,coNP), valid-inequality testing is NP-complete, and extension complexity is at least $1.5^n$. Our hardness results yield, as a special case, a result of Crama and of Gallo and Simone. Furthermore, our hardness results also explain the lack of any good characterization of the extreme rays of the cone of $k$-additive $(k{-}2)$-monotone games.
item.dc:creator: Michel Grabisch and. Hans Raj Tiwary

item.title: Sensitivity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions via Binary Necklaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.17006v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Rotation symmetric Boolean functions are important structured families in the theory of Boolean functions, where cyclic invariance permits compact algebraic descriptions while retaining nontrivial local behavior. We investigate their sensitivity through binary necklaces and monomial orbit sums. In the necklace quotient of the Boolean cube, ordinary adjacency does not record the number of coordinate flips: we give a directed flip-multiplicity formula involving stabilizers and distance-two near-periods, and derive exact local sensitivity formulas when the number of variables is an odd prime. For monomial rotation symmetric functions we determine sensitivity for all odd degrees and for quadratic orbit sums. For the consecutive-monomial family of every even degree $d\ge4$, we prove a run-cluster inequality and obtain the eventual exact formula $s(F_{d,n})=n-\min\{r,d+2-r\}$, where $n\equiv r\pmod{d+2}$, under the stated length hypothesis. The consecutive quartic case follows explicitly. We also evaluate sensitivity for cyclic run-threshold functions. Our results provide exact combinatorial and complexity-theoretic information about cyclic Boolean functions and clarify how cyclic symmetry governs local sensitivity.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Li, Jing Zhang

item.title: Block Sensitivity and Certificate Complexity of Rotation Symmetric Boolean Functions
item.description: arXiv:2610.17100v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate block sensitivity and certificate complexity of monomial rotation-symmetric Boolean functions, obtaining exact formulas and structural classifications for several families. For odd-degree monomial rotation-symmetric functions, the equality $s(f)=n$ established in our earlier work yields $bs(f)=C(f)=n$. For quadratic monomial rotation-symmetric functions, we determine both measures completely and prove that block sensitivity equals certificate complexity. For consecutive quartic monomials, we determine sensitivity, block sensitivity, and certificate complexity in every residue class of the number of variables. Our principal result is an exact global block-sensitivity formula for consecutive monomials of every even degree $d\ge4$. Writing $n=q(d+2)+\rho$, where $0\le\rho<d+2$ and $q\ge\max\{2,d/2-1\}$, we prove \[ bs(F_{d,n})=n-\min\left\{\left\lceil\frac{\rho}{2}\right\rceil,d+2-\rho\right\}. \] We also establish the corresponding sensitivity formula by a self-contained argument, yielding arbitrarily large gaps between sensitivity and block sensitivity as the degree varies. For certificate complexity, we obtain exact pointwise formulas for structured run-and-gap configurations and establish additional global equalities, including $C(F_{6,8q+5})=bs(F_{6,8q+5})=8q+2$ for $q\ge2$. Our methods combine cyclic run decomposition, parity arguments, explicit sensitive-block constructions, and constant-subcube certificates. The exact global certificate complexity for arbitrary even degrees remains open.
item.dc:creator: Yuan Li, Jing Zhang
